title: Protecting Britain’s satellites: threats, resilience and what to do now
label: 19 October 2026 · Space resilience
summary: Witnesses from academia, industry and a composites centre explained how the UK’s growing reliance on satellites exposes it to jamming, cyber attacks, supply‑chain pressure and space weather. They urged faster, more diverse and more practical resilience: more small satellites, stronger cyber protection for ground systems, closer European partnerships, use of commercial capability for rapid sovereign launches, and clearer government leadership and auditing of legacy systems.

chapters.title: How satellites matter and what resilience looks like
chapters.takeaway: Satellites underpin huge parts of the economy and security; resilience comes from many small, replaceable systems, strong ground defences and fast reconstitution.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. To open: how do you see the threat picture, and does the new UK Space Strategy match that?

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: Planet runs large fleets of Earth‑imaging satellites used for environment and security—Ukraine uses our data daily. Resilience for us rests on three things: many small satellites, close work with governments about threats, and the ability to launch replacements rapidly.

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: We can build satellites very quickly—roughly 40 per week at peak—so you can have sovereign-owned satellites launched in months, not years. That gives speed and control together.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the UK strategy show urgency?

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: It sets useful aims but lacks urgency and timelines. Some national projects like ISTARI may finish too late—2035—for today's threats.

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: Space underpins about 18% of UK GDP and around £450bn of activity. We are getting more dependent as satellite numbers grow from ~12,000 to maybe 60,000 by 2030, so we need contingency planning for cascading failures.

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: A structural problem is accountability: many departments use space but no single body is clearly responsible for national resilience and cross‑government response at the ‘speed of relevance’.

chapters.title: Real examples of hostile action and low‑cost disruptions
chapters.takeaway: State actors have targeted space-related systems already; ground facilities and small disruptive acts can have outsized effects.

turns.speaker: Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi
turns.text: How willing and able are adversaries to disrupt the UK’s space infrastructure? Any recent evidence?

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: Ukraine shows the risk: Russia has jammed and attacked networks. Commercial providers can be targeted but can also help because they’re flexible—Planet supplied Ukraine directly unlike some systems that were constrained by other governments.

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: We’ve seen cyber intrusions into military ground sites in the UK. The Viasat attack before the 2022 invasion targeted communications and affected many civilian users too. Ground infrastructure is the most accessible and vulnerable part of space systems.

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: Watch also for close approaches by other nations’ satellites. For example, a Russian satellite manoeuvred to within about 26 metres of a commercial satellite—very close and a worrying pattern.

turns.speaker: Lord Godson
turns.text: What about threats beyond Russia—China, Iran, dark horses?

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: China is a major actor; Iran is increasingly capable and could collaborate with others. But the near-term big multiplier will be AI‑enabled cyber attacks that scale much faster than nation-state kinetic actions.

chapters.title: Cyber, AI and the increasing digital threat
chapters.takeaway: Cyber attacks—made faster and more capable by AI—are a primary and growing threat to satellites, especially via ground systems and supply chains.

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: Cyber threats are becoming easier and more common. Satellites and their ground control, user terminals and supply chains all have vulnerabilities. AI tools can make attacks cheaper and more effective.

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: Small organisations running CubeSats or university projects are especially at risk: a compromised small satellite could be used to create collisions or debris, with wider consequences.

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: I agree. AI is accelerating capability—the last two years saw huge advances in large language models. Those same advances will power cyber attacks unless we set guardrails and verification, and that affects space like any other critical infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: Another problem: organisations often don’t publicly say when they've been hit, so we lack visibility of attacks and the lessons to defend against them.

turns.speaker: Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom
turns.text: Is the 5–25% chance of a major space‑weather event in the National Risk Register reliable?

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: Be cautious about putting precise probabilities on rare catastrophes. Space weather is unpredictable: we are in a solar maximum now and solar activity can be much higher than models expect.

chapters.title: Supply chains, partners and sovereign options
chapters.takeaway: The UK should diversify partners, lean on EU collaboration, use commercial providers for fast sovereign capability, and defend supply chains and ground systems.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Can we rely on US supply and support, and should we work more with the EU?

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: Work with both. Europe is a natural security partner, and having manufacturing and control in Europe gives independence from US regulatory or political constraints. Planet builds in the US and Germany and operates ground stations in the UK.

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: Diversity is the resilience strategy: use NATO and bilateral links, be at the table for EU defence/space rules, and keep options to reconstitute assets quickly through partners.

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: Commercial providers can deliver sovereign satellites fast—Sweden had a first sovereign satellite in four months with Planet. The UK should adopt similar hybrid approaches: commercial plus sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Where are the main vulnerabilities in our ground estate and launches?

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: Ground stations, control centres and limited domestic launch options are weak points. New UK spaceports like SaxaVord help polar launches, but heavy or equatorial launches still rely on allies and costly rockets like Ariane.

chapters.title: Space weather, legacy satellites and practical resilience
chapters.takeaway: Space weather can damage fleets; many old satellites can’t be retrofitted, so the UK needs audits, contingency plans and to fund upgrades and rapid replacement capability.

turns.speaker: Helen Maguire
turns.text: How big a risk is space weather, and what would the impact look like?

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: A big solar storm could cause wide radio interference, damage electronics and increase atmospheric drag causing satellite loss. Attribution is hard—weather can look like attack, which adds ambiguity in crisis.

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: In the recent solar maximum some companies lost large fractions of their fleets because drag rose unexpectedly. Better modelling and designing satellites for those events help; radiation hardening is also possible with government-backed R&D.

turns.speaker: Lord Sedwill
turns.text: Can we retrofit existing satellites to be more resilient?

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: Retrofitting thousands of fast-moving satellites is extremely challenging and costly. For current satellites, detection and contingency plans are more realistic than mass retrofits.

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: The strategy mentions in‑orbit assembly and RPO as future options; those techniques may eventually let us service or refuel satellites, but they’re years away.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is there an audit of the UK’s legacy satellite dependence and what to replace?

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: I don’t have evidence of a public, comprehensive audit. I can follow up on what exists and how academia and industry could help map dependence and capabilities.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please do write to the committee on that and on how UK research can be better mobilised.

turns.speaker: Will Marshall
turns.text: Quick final point: commercial satellite fleets and partnerships let the UK get faster sovereign capability—if government moves faster and funds targeted R&D, resilience gains can follow quickly.

turns.speaker: Dr Julia Balm
turns.text: And institutionally: the UK needs clearer roles, better information sharing across departments and to stay engaged with allies and EU rule‑making to shape collective resilience.

turns.speaker: Jessie Hamill-Stewart
turns.text: Also fund and clear pathways for smaller companies and universities to work with government—security clearance and procurement barriers stop valuable expertise contributing to space cyber defence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all—very informative. We’ll follow up on audits and academic capability.
